CausalPy method: SyntheticControl



Synthetic control is a method for estimating causal effects in comparative case studies where a single treated unit is compared to a weighted combination of control units (Abadie et al. 2010). The key idea is to construct a “synthetic” control that closely matches the treated unit’s pre-intervention trajectory.
This notebook covers the Texas prison reform example from Cunningham (2021), which examines the effect of prison capacity expansion on incarceration rates.

title: Chapter 10: Synthetic Control
text:
CausalPy Synthetic Control Analysis
Now we use CausalPy’s SyntheticControl to estimate the treatment effect. CausalPy will:

Find optimal weights for donor states that best match Texas pre-1993
Construct the synthetic Texas using these weights
Compare actual Texas to synthetic Texas post-1993

CausalPy 1.0 scales the observation-noise prior from the treated unit’s pre-treatment spread (auto_scale_sigma=True, the default). That replaces the old fixed HalfNormal(1) prior, so posterior magnitudes will not match a pre-1.0 run. This page keeps the default.

# Run Synthetic Control with CausalPy
result = cp.SyntheticControl(
    df_wide,
    treatment_time,
    control_units=control_units,
    treated_units=[treated_unit],
    model=cp.pymc_models.WeightedSumFitter(
        sample_kwargs={
            "tune": 1000,
            "draws": 1000,
            "chains": 4,
            "cores": 4,
            "target_accept": 0.95,
            "progressbar": True,
            "random_seed": 42,
        }
    ),
).fit()

text:
Treatment Effect (Gap Plot)
The treatment effect is the difference between actual Texas and synthetic Texas. This “gap plot” shows the causal effect over time.

# Get the post-treatment impact
post_impact = result.result.impact_post

# Plot the gap (treatment effect over time)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 6))

# Get posterior mean for the impact
impact_mean = post_impact.mean(dim=["chain", "draw"]).values.flatten()

# Get HDI using percentiles directly
impact_lower = post_impact.quantile(0.03, dim=["chain", "draw"]).values.flatten()
impact_upper = post_impact.quantile(0.97, dim=["chain", "draw"]).values.flatten()

years_post = result.datapost.index.values

# Plot mean impact with uncertainty
ax.fill_between(
    years_post,
    impact_lower,
    impact_upper,
    alpha=0.3,
    color="C0",
    label="94% CI",
)
ax.plot(years_post, impact_mean, color="C0", linewidth=2, label="Mean effect")

# Add zero line
ax.axhline(y=0, color="black", linestyle="--", alpha=0.5)

# Add treatment time
ax.axvline(
    x=treatment_time,
    color="red",
    linestyle="--",
    linewidth=2,
    label=f"Treatment ({treatment_time})",
)

ax.set_xlabel("Year", fontsize=12)
ax.set_ylabel("Treatment Effect (Actual - Synthetic)", fontsize=12)
ax.set_title("Texas Prison Reform: Causal Effect on Incarceration", fontsize=14)

title: Chapter 10: Synthetic Control
text:
Effect Summary
CausalPy provides a convenient effect_summary() method for decision-ready reporting.

# Generate effect summary
stats = result.effect_summary(treated_unit=treated_unit)
print(stats.text)

During the Post-period (1993.0 to 2000.0), the response variable had an average value of approx. 52733.88. By contrast, in the absence of an intervention, we would have expected an average response of 10255.57. The 95% interval of this counterfactual prediction is [6935.17, 13876.31]. Subtracting this prediction from the observed response yields an estimate of the causal effect the intervention had on the response variable. This effect is 42478.30 with a 95% interval of [38857.56, 45798.70].

Summing up the individual data points during the Post-period, the response variable had an overall value of 421871.00. By contrast, had the intervention not taken place, we would have expected a sum of 82044.58. The 95% interval of this prediction is [55481.40, 111010.49]. The cumulative effect is 339826.42 with a 95% HDI [310860.51, 366389.60].

The posterior probability of an increase is 1.000. For the cumulative effect, The posterior probability of an increase is 1.000. Relative to the counterfactual, the effect represents a 430.61% change (95% HDI [265.29%, 621.54%]).

This analysis assumes that the control units used to construct the synthetic counterfactual were not themselves affected by the intervention, and that the pre-treatment relationship between control and treated units remains stable throughout the post-treatment period. We recommend inspecting model fit, examining pre-intervention trends, and conducting sensitivity analyses (e.g., placebo tests) to support any causal conclusions drawn from this analysis.

title: Chapter 10: Synthetic Control
text:
Placebo-in-Space Tests
One key diagnostic for synthetic control is the placebo test. The idea is:

Pretend each donor state was actually treated at the same time
Run synthetic control for that “placebo treated” state
Calculate the post-treatment gap (placebo effect)
Compare the actual Texas effect to the distribution of placebo effects

If Texas’s effect is unusually large compared to placebos, we have stronger evidence that the effect is real.
This corresponds to synth_3_7.R in the Mixtape, which uses R’s generate.placebos() function.

# Run placebo tests on a subset of donor states
# (Running all 50 would be time-consuming, so we select a representative subset)

# Select states with reasonable data (no missing values, reasonable scale)
placebo_states = [
    "California",
    "Florida",
    "New York",
    "Illinois",
    "Ohio",
    "Pennsylvania",
    "Michigan",
    "Georgia",
    "North Carolina",
    "Virginia",
]

# Store results
placebo_gaps = {}
texas_gap = result.result.impact_post.mean(dim=["chain", "draw"]).values.flatten()

print("Running placebo tests (this may take a few minutes)...")
print("-" * 50)

for state in placebo_states:
    print(f"Testing placebo: {state}...", end=" ")

    # Define control pool (all states except the placebo treated state)
    placebo_controls = [s for s in all_states if s != state]

    try:
        # Run synthetic control with this state as "treated"
        placebo_result = cp.SyntheticControl(
            df_wide,
            treatment_time,
            control_units=placebo_controls,
            treated_units=[state],
            model=cp.pymc_models.WeightedSumFitter(
                sample_kwargs={
                    "tune": 500,  # Faster for placebo tests
                    "draws": 500,
                    "chains": 4,
                    "cores": 4,
                    "target_accept": 0.9,
                    "progressbar": False,
                    "random_seed": 42,
                }
            ),
        ).fit()

        # Store the mean gap
        gap = placebo_result.result.impact_post.mean(dim=["chain", "draw"]).values.flatten()
        placebo_gaps[state] = gap
        print(f"Mean gap: {np.mean(gap):.1f}")

    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Error: {e}")

print("-" * 50)
print(f"Completed {len(placebo_gaps)} placebo tests")

title: Chapter 8: Panel Data
text:
Mixtape chapter: Panel Data
CausalPy method: PanelRegression



Pooled OLS treats every client session as a separate draw. If providers who take riskier sessions also differ in ways that do not change across their sessions — and those differences affect price — the provider effect sits in the error and the slopes are biased.
The within estimator, which is what provider fixed effects estimate, subtracts each provider’s mean. That deletes the time-invariant unit effect (u_i). A slope is then identified only from within-provider variation. Two conditions have to hold: the idiosyncratic error is strictly exogenous given the unit effect, and the regressor actually moves inside the provider. A covariate that is constant for each provider is wiped, not estimated.






Important



Fixed effects are not a fix for reverse causality, and they are not a fix for a confounder that changes across sessions. The chapter shows those failures with published tables from Cornwell and Trumbull (1994) and Cornwell and Rupert (1997). Those datasets are not in the Mixtape repo. This page cites the tables and does not recreate them.


The coded exercise is Cunningham and Kendall’s Survey of Adult Service Providers. Each row is one of a provider’s recent client sessions, not a calendar year. The outcome is log hourly price (lnw). Table 8.3 reports three columns on the same balanced sample: pooled OLS, provider fixed effects, and OLS on provider-demeaned variables. Columns 2 and 3 are the same point estimates. That equivalence is the result to show. The book does not put session fixed effects in this regression.

text:
Three point estimates
Same sklearn backend for all three columns, so a difference is the estimator, not the optimizer. PanelRegression requires unit_fe_variable, so pooled OLS cannot be that class. It is LinearRegression on the formula design matrix, with fit_intercept=False because patsy already built the intercept column. CausalPy does the same internally.
time_fe_variable stays unset. On the demeaned path that argument is not a label: setting it also demeans by that column, which would be two-way FE. The book is one-way provider FE. Session is the within-unit index, not a second fixed effect.
The demeaned formula keeps only the time-varying regressors. After demeaning, the provider characteristics are zero columns and the design is singular. Leaving them out is the result, not a shorter model.

pooled_formula = "lnw ~ " + " + ".join(REGRESSORS)
dummy_formula = "lnw ~ C(id) + " + " + ".join(REGRESSORS)
demeaned_formula = "lnw ~ " + " + ".join(TIME_VARYING)

if "session" in pooled_formula or "C(session)" in dummy_formula or "C(session)" in demeaned_formula:
    raise RuntimeError("estimating formulas must not include session fixed effects")
for column in TIME_INVARIANT:
    if column in demeaned_formula.split(" ~ ", 1)[1].split(" + "):
        raise RuntimeError(f"{column} is time-invariant and does not belong in the demeaned formula")

y_pooled, X_pooled = build_formula_matrices(pooled_formula, sasp)
pooled_fit = LinearRegression(fit_intercept=False).fit(
    np.asarray(X_pooled), np.asarray(y_pooled).ravel()
)
pooled_slopes = dict(zip(X_pooled.design_info.column_names, pooled_fit.coef_))

fe = cp.PanelRegression(
    sasp,
    dummy_formula,
    unit_fe_variable="id",
    time_fe_variable=None,
    fe_method="dummies",
    model=LinearRegression(fit_intercept=False),
).fit()
within = cp.PanelRegression(
    sasp,
    demeaned_formula,
    unit_fe_variable="id",
    time_fe_variable=None,
    fe_method="demeaned",
    model=LinearRegression(fit_intercept=False),
).fit()


def coefficient_means(result):
    """Mean coefficient by patsy label.

    PanelRegression keeps draws on the model backend rather than a result
    bundle. An OLS backend is one draw, so the mean is the point estimate.
    """
    draws = result._model_backend.coefficients()
    return {
        str(name): float(draws.sel(coeffs=name).mean())
        for name in draws.coords["coeffs"].values
    }


fe_slopes = coefficient_means(fe)
within_slopes = coefficient_means(within)

if fe.time_fe_variable is not None or within.time_fe_variable is not None:
    raise RuntimeError("estimating fits must leave time_fe_variable unset")

for term in TIME_VARYING:
    if abs(fe_slopes[term] - within_slopes[term]) > 1e-8:
        raise RuntimeError(f"{term}: dummy FE and demeaned FE differ")

for term, (ols_target, fe_target) in BOOK.items():
    if round(pooled_slopes[term], 3) != ols_target:
        raise RuntimeError(f"{term} pooled OLS {pooled_slopes[term]:.6f} != {ols_target}")
    if round(fe_slopes[term], 3) != fe_target or round(within_slopes[term], 3) != fe_target:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"{term} FE {fe_slopes[term]:.6f} / demeaned {within_slopes[term]:.6f} != {fe_target}"

Provider fixed effects and the within transformation answer the same point-estimate question, and only that question. They delete time-invariant confounding. import warnings

import numpy as np

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

import causalpy as cp

# Add the src directory to path for our data utilities
import sys

title: Chapter 6: Regression Discontinuity
text:
Part 1: RD Concepts via Simulation
Before diving into real data, let’s build intuition for regression discontinuity using simulated examples (rdd_simulate1-4).
Data-generating process adapted from python/rdd_simulate1.py in the Mixtape code repository. See NOTICE.

# rdd_simulate1 & rdd_simulate2: Treatment effect simulations
sim_dat = pd.DataFrame({"x": np.random.normal(50, 25, 1000)})
sim_dat.loc[sim_dat.x < 0, "x"] = 0
sim_dat = sim_dat[sim_dat.x < 100]
sim_dat["D"] = (sim_dat.x > 50).astype(int)

# Y1: No treatment effect | Y2: Treatment effect = 40
sim_dat["y1"] = (
    25 + 0 * sim_dat.D + 1.5 * sim_dat.x + np.random.normal(0, 20, len(sim_dat))
)
sim_dat["y2"] = (
    25 + 40 * sim_dat.D + 1.5 * sim_dat.x + np.random.normal(0, 20, len(sim_dat))
)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))
for ax, y_col, title in [
    (axes[0], "y1", "No Treatment Effect"),
    (axes[1], "y2", "Treatment Effect = 40"),
]:
    colors = ["C0" if d == 0 else "C3" for d in sim_dat.D]
    ax.scatter(sim_dat.x, sim_dat[y_col], c=colors, alpha=0.5, s=20)
    for d, color in [(0, "C0"), (1, "C3")]:
        subset = sim_dat[sim_dat.D == d]
        z = np.polyfit(subset.x, subset[y_col], 1)
        x_line = np.linspace(subset.x.min(), subset.x.max(), 100)
        ax.plot(x_line, np.polyval(z, x_line), color=color, linewidth=2)
    ax.axvline(x=50, color="gray", linestyle="--", linewidth=2)
    ax.set_xlabel("Test Score (X)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Outcome (Y)")
    ax.set_title(title)
plt.suptitle("RD Simulations: The Discontinuity Reveals the Treatment Effect", y=1.02)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









# rdd_simulate3: Nonlinear CEF - Linear fit creates FALSE discontinuity
sim_nonlin = pd.DataFrame({"x": np.random.normal(100, 50, 1000)})
sim_nonlin.loc[sim_nonlin.x < 0, "x"] = 0
sim_nonlin["D"] = (sim_nonlin.x > 140).astype(int)
sim_nonlin["y"] = (
    10000
    - 100 * sim_nonlin.x
    + sim_nonlin.x**2
    + np.random.normal(0, 1000, len(sim_nonlin))
)
sim_nonlin = sim_nonlin[sim_nonlin.x < 280]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))
colors = ["C0" if d == 0 else "C3" for d in sim_nonlin.D]
for ax, deg, title in [
    (axes[0], 1, "Linear: FALSE Discontinuity!"),
    (axes[1], 2, "Quadratic: Correct (No Effect)"),
]:
    ax.scatter(sim_nonlin.x, sim_nonlin.y, c=colors, alpha=0.2, s=20)
    for d, color in [(0, "C0"), (1, "C3")]:
        subset = sim_nonlin[sim_nonlin.D == d]
        z = np.polyfit(subset.x, subset.y, deg)
        x_line = np.linspace(subset.x.min(), subset.x.max(), 100)
        ax.plot(x_line, np.polyval(z, x_line), color=color, linewidth=2)
    ax.axvline(x=140, color="gray", linestyle="--", linewidth=2)
    ax.set_xlabel("Running Variable (X)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Outcome (Y)")
    ax.set_title(title)
plt.suptitle(
    "Danger of Nonlinearity: Use Flexible Functional Forms or Focus Near Threshold",
    y=1.02,
)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









# rdd_simulate4: no discontinuity. Reset the seed so this cell matches the
# script's DGP rather than continuing the stream from simulate1-3.
np.random.seed(12282020)
sim4 = pd.DataFrame({"x": np.random.normal(100, 50, 1000)})
sim4.loc[sim4.x < 0, "x"] = 0
sim4["x2"] = sim4["x"] ** 2
sim4["x3"] = sim4["x"] ** 3
sim4["D"] = (sim4["x"] > 140).astype(int)
sim4["y3"] = (
    10000
    + 0 * sim4["D"]
    - 100 * sim4["x"]
    + sim4["x"] ** 2
    + np.random.normal(0, 1000, 1000)
)
sim4 = sim4[sim4.x < 280]
sim4_fit = smf.ols(
    "y3 ~ D + x + x2 + x3 + D*x + D*x2 + D*x3", data=sim4
).fit()
sim4_d = float(sim4_fit.params["D"])
# The formula's D coefficient is the intercept gap at x=0. The jump the
# figure is about is the predicted difference at the cutoff.
cutoff = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "x": [140.0, 140.0],
        "x2": [140.0**2, 140.0**2],
        "x3": [140.0**3, 140.0**3],
        "D": [0, 1],
    }
)
sim4_jump = float(np.diff(sim4_fit.predict(cutoff))[0])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
colors = ["C0" if d == 0 else "C3" for d in sim4["D"]]
ax.scatter(sim4["x"], sim4["y3"], c=colors, alpha=0.25, s=16)
for d, color in [(0, "C0"), (1, "C3")]:
    side = sim4[sim4["D"] == d].sort_values("x")
    ax.plot(side["x"], sim4_fit.predict(side), color=color, linewidth=2)
ax.axvline(x=140, color="gray", linestyle="--", linewidth=2)
ax.set_xlabel("Running variable (X)")
ax.set_ylabel("Outcome (Y)")
ax.set_title("No planted jump: flexible fit")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
print(f"Formula D coefficient (intercept gap at x=0): {sim4_d:.1f}")
print(f"Predicted gap at the cutoff x=140: {sim4_jump:.1f}")







Figure 1: Simulated outcome with a smooth conditional expectation and no planted jump at 140. Curves are the fully interacted polynomial fit on each side of the cutoff.





Formula D coefficient (intercept gap at x=0): -11893.4
Predicted gap at the cutoff x=140: 180.6


The data-generating process plants a jump of zero at 140. The script’s formula is y3 ~ D * (x + x2 + x3), so its D coefficient is the intercept gap at x = 0, not the jump at the cutoff. The same fit’s predicted gap at 140 is 181, against an outcome near 15,000 and noise with standard deviation 1,000. A linear fit on each side of a curved conditional expectation can still look like a discontinuity; that failure is the previous simulation, not this one.

# CausalPy bandwidth sensitivity analysis
bandwidths = [0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.25]
bw_results = []

for bw in bandwidths:
    try:
        res = cp.RegressionDiscontinuity(
            data=df_clean,
            formula="score ~ 1 + demvoteshare_c + treated",
            running_variable_name="demvoteshare_c",
            model=cp.pymc_models.LinearRegression(
                sample_kwargs={"progressbar": False, "random_seed": 42}
            ),
            treatment_threshold=0.0,
            bandwidth=bw,
        ).fit()
        disc = res.result.discontinuity_at_threshold
        eff = float(disc.mean())
        sd = float(disc.std())
        n = len(df_clean[df_clean["demvoteshare_c"].abs() <= bw])
        bw_results.append({"bw": bw, "n": n, "effect": eff, "sd": sd})
        print(f"BW={bw:.2f}: n={n:5d}, effect={eff:.1f} ± {sd:.1f}")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"BW={bw:.2f}: Error - {e}")

Example 3: Inverse Propensity Weighting with CausalPy
Now we’ll use CausalPy’s InversePropensityWeighting to estimate the treatment effect using an observational control group (CPS data) instead of the experimental control group.

The Challenge
When we replace the experimental control group with CPS controls, the simple difference in outcomes will be heavily biased because the CPS sample differs systematically from NSW participants (in age, education, earnings history, etc.).


The Solution
Inverse Propensity Weighting (IPW) reweights observations to create a “pseudo-population” where treatment assignment is independent of observed covariates.

# Load CPS control data

The LaLonde Problem
The famous LaLonde (1986) paper showed that observational estimators often fail to recover the experimental benchmark. The NSW treated group was very different from CPS controls:

Lower prior earnings: NSW participants were disadvantaged workers
Different demographics: More minority, less educated
Selection into treatment: Voluntary program participation

IPW attempts to correct for these differences by reweighting, but: - Limited overlap can cause extreme weights - Model misspecification affects results - No adjustment for unobservables


This run
Robust IPW on the NSW treated units plus CPS controls, random_seed=42: ATE -12,231.26 dollars, posterior sd 341.34 dollars, interval [-12,900.29, -11,562.23] dollars. That interval is the mean plus or minus 1.96 posterior standard deviations from the 200 draws in the cell above, not a new estimator. The experimental benchmark on this page is 1,794 dollars. The observational estimate does not recover it. A pre-1.0 run of the same cell was about -12,265 dollars, so the migration did not move this estimate off the LaLonde failure. The book’s logit is not this specification: it includes polynomials, an educ * re74 interaction, and a 0.1–0.9 trim. Those terms are not added here, and no rows are dropped to imitate the trim. InversePropensityWeighting has no trim argument and no ATT argument. Dropping rows outside 0.1–0.9 would be a hand edit, not a feature of the class.







NoteNot estimated



Subclassification (titanic_subclassification.py), nearest-neighbor matching (teffects_nn.py), and coarsened exact matching (cem.py) are not in CausalPy. The last two scripts are empty in the Mixtape repository. None of the three is run here, and no pandas or R matcher is built. The write-up is proposals/proposal_matching.md. teffects_ipw.py is not a section of the 2021 chapter, so it is not added either.

Summary
In this notebook, we demonstrated:

Simple Difference in Outcomes: The Titanic example shows that naive comparisons can be misleading when treatment is not randomly assigned.
Experimental Benchmark: The NSW randomized experiment provides an unbiased ATE estimate (~$1,794) that serves as our ground truth.

Key takeaways:

IPW is one approach to addressing selection bias in observational studies
CausalPy provides Bayesian propensity score estimation with uncertainty quantification
Balance diagnostics help assess whether weighting achieves covariate balance
The LaLonde problem remains challenging — observational methods may not fully recover experimental estimates

CausalPy Instrumental Variable Analysis
Now we use CausalPy’s InstrumentalVariable experiment to estimate the causal effect of education on wages, using nearc4 as an instrument.
CausalPy implements IV as a Bayesian model that jointly estimates the two stages. Both stages include the controls from card.py: exper, black, south, married, and smsa.

Second stage: lwage ~ educ + exper + black + south + married + smsa

The Mixtape’s IV analysis of the Card data shows:

Notes on the IV Estimate
The IV estimate is often larger than OLS for returns to schooling. This seems counterintuitive (we expect ability bias to inflate OLS), but there are several explanations:

Measurement error: OLS is attenuated by measurement error in education; IV corrects this
Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE): IV estimates the effect for “compliers” — people whose education is actually affected by college proximity. This group may have higher returns than average.
Heterogeneous effects: The marginal return to schooling for those on the margin of attending college may be higher

Judge fixed-effects example
python/bail.py is the judge-leniency design. One Bayesian fit is shown, with the script’s minimum controls. The maximum-control specification is not fit. JIVE is not ported.
jail3 is the treatment. guilt is the outcome. judge_pre_1 through judge_pre_7 are the instruments. bailDate is converted to days since 1970-01-01. day, day2, and that day count are then centered and divided by their standard deviation. The default outcome-stage prior is a normal centered on the 2SLS coefficients with scale 1 for every coefficient. On the raw day-squared column, which runs to about 394,000, that scale is enormous relative to the coefficient, and the design is ill-conditioned. The scaling is affine, so the jail3 coefficient is the same contrast as in the script. t1 through t5 stay as indicators. The book’s estimator is linear 2SLS, so binary_treatment=False. plot() raises NotImplementedError and is not called. nuts_sampler is omitted, so nutpie is selected. No cores argument is passed.

Overview
Adoption dates in the castle-doctrine panel are not a single year. A two-group, two-period coefficient is the wrong estimand for that design, and it is not what this page reports.
The required fit below is the Borusyak, Jaravel, and Spiess imputation estimator (Borusyak et al. 2024). The untreated outcome is sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression on state and year fixed effects. It is not Cheng and Hoekstra’s two-way fixed-effects coefficient (Cheng and Hoekstra 2013), and it is not castle_1.py. A short Bayesian sample of the same formula is optional. It is not the required result.
Snow, the minimum wage, block bootstrap, clustering, the Affordable Care Act, and maternity benefits have no script on this page. No dataset is added for them.

The file stores a missing treatment_date for 29 states. StaggeredDifferenceInDifferences rejects missing treatment times. It does not read a missing date as never-treated. Those dates are recoded to np.inf, the class default for never-treated, before the fit. The states stay in the panel and are the never-treated controls. None are dropped.

Imputation event-time contrasts
The required formula is state and year fixed effects. C() accepts the numeric year column, so year is not recoded to a string. The 1 in the formula is the intercept column of the design matrix. sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression fits that matrix. It does not add a second intercept.
post is an absorbing 0/1 column in the file. It is not passed as treated_variable_name. The absorbing-treatment check runs only when that argument is passed. l_homicide has no missing values, so there is nothing for a missing-outcome check to drop. The class’s missing-value check on a treated column is about the treatment indicator, not the outcome.
StaggeredDifferenceInDifferences has no weight argument. popwt is not passed, and this is not the book’s population-weighted least squares.

NoteWhat this fit is not



This is not castle_1.py. That script is population-weighted least squares of log homicide on post, demographic and spending covariates, region-quarter indicators, state trends, and state and year effects, with standard errors clustered by state. This page does not estimate that coefficient. The class has no weight argument, so popwt is not used.
castle_2.py is an event study: leads 1–9 and lags 1–5, with lag0 omitted, plus region-quarter indicators and state and year effects. It is population-weighted least squares, clustered by state. It does not include castle_1.py’s covariate list. castle_3.py and castle_4.py plot those weighted least-squares estimates. CausalPy does not implement that regression. The sklearn table above is the imputation substitute, not those figures.
castle_5.py is empty. The R script decomposes l_homicide ~ post with the Bacon decomposition. It is not run.
PR #584 is an open proposal for a common-timing event study. It is not this staggered design, and it is not a castle-doctrine specification.








NoteBacon decomposition and triple differences



A Bacon decomposition would split a two-way fixed-effects coefficient into timing comparisons. CausalPy does not implement it, and none is computed. This file also has no already-treated cohort in 2000.
Triple differences (abortion_ddd.py, abortion_ddd2.py) are not in CausalPy. The write-up is proposals/proposal_triple_diff.md. That proposal is not a Bacon decomposition.
